Where it began

Alastair Cook was born in Gloucester on Christmas Day 1984 and grew up in Wickham Bishops, a village in Essex. Music came first: he was learning the clarinet by eight and boarded at St Paul's Cathedral School in London as a chorister. In the holidays he played for Maldon Cricket Club, turning out for their adult third eleven at 11.

His musical gifts took him to Bedford School as a boarder at 13, and cricket soon took over. When the MCC arrived a man short for a match against the school, they borrowed the 14-year-old new boy, who promptly made a hundred against his own side. His last summer there brought 1,287 runs at an average of 160.87, a school record. He joined the Essex academy at 16 and made his first-class debut for the county in 2003.

The player

England called him up in a hurry in 2006, flying him from an academy tour of the West Indies to India. Aged 21, he made 60 and then an unbeaten 104 on debut, and that hundred was the 3,000th in Test history. Between 2006 and 2018 he played 161 Tests, making 12,472 runs at 45.35 with 33 hundreds and a best of 294 against India in 2011.

The 2010–11 Ashes was his masterpiece: 766 runs, including 235 not out at Brisbane, and more than 36 hours at the crease across the series. He took over the Test captaincy in 2012, led England in 59 Tests, and that winter took them to a first series win in India since 1984–85, with a hundred in each of his first three Tests in charge there.

What made him special

His great strength was concentration. With a compact method he wore bowlers down rather than knocking them over, and he could bat for hour after hour. He also held 175 catches, some of them at short leg, where bravery is part of the job.

The fast lane was never his. One-day selectors overlooked him for long spells early on, and he was once judged too slow for Twenty20. Bowling was not his department either, though nobody can argue with his figures: one Test wicket, at a cost of just seven runs.

Away from the middle

He was made an MBE in 2011 and a CBE in 2016, and in the 2019 New Year Honours he was knighted for services to cricket. He was a Wisden Cricketer of the Year and joined the ICC Hall of Fame in 2023. After leaving Tests he carried on with Essex, helping them win the 2019 County Championship, made his 70th first-class hundred in 2022, and turned to commentary on Test Match Special.

And finally

At Bedford he was President of the Music Society as well as cricket captain. Bowlers who spent whole days trying to get him out might say he simply found another way to make them dance to his tune.
